Zombie Wars BY JODY DUNCAN he film adaptation of Max Brooks' apocalyptic zombie invasion novel World War Z: An Oral History of the Zombie War was - in the old parlance - 'in the can' when Paramount Pictures, director Marc Forster and producer/star Brad Pitt made the controversial decision to throw out much of the film's third act, and rewrite and reshoot a new one. It was a bold move with a simple rationale: the third act, as it existed, just wasn't good enough. "They had shot this whole sequence in Budapest," explained visual effects supervisor Scott Farrar, "which was supposed to be Russia in the story. Originally, the premise was that the action of the movie started in warm weather; and then, by the end, you're in Russia and the weather has turned cold, and something about the cold makes the zombies slow down, so they are easier to kill - and that's what gives people a fighting chance against them. But the sequence didn't make a lot of sense, and didn't resonate emotionally. So everybody got together, and said, 'This isn't working, and so we're not going to use any of the ending that we shot.' It was a very brave and tough decision Screenwriter Damon Lindelof, of television's Lost and J.J. Abrams' Star Trek Into I / 25 Darkness, wrote a new ending, which the filmmakers shot at Pinewood Studios in October,

WORLD WAR Z November and December of 2012, wrapping just six months prior to the film's June 28 release date. The rewrite and subsequent reshoot were codas on a production that had seen its share of troubles, documented in industry media outlets and in a lengthy article in Vanity fair. But the final result was an exciting new take on the genre, and a critical thumbs-up rarely afforded a movie of the zombie persuasion. Singled out for praise were the zombies themselves, which were the product of a long evolutionary process that started early in 2011 with concepts by Legacy Effects.We were brought in to come up with ideas of what these zombies would look likei said Legacy supervisor John Rosengrant.The idea was to make them look very organic and realistic, like a forensically accurate execution of what an 'undead' person might look like, depending on the trauma he'd suffered and how long he'd been dead." Concept work was also being done across the pond, at Framestore, which had just recently created a visual development department as a separate unit, under the supervision of Kevin Jenkins. "Initially," said Jenkins, "we were hired to work with production designer Nigel Phelps in developing the look of this world, but our job evolved to creating concepts for the zombie. From the outset, I said, 'You can't redesign a zombie, so let's not even try.' And everyone looked at me like I was some sort of madman. I said: 'This is a rare situation - a zombie movie with money behind it. Rather than having 18 people in zombie clothes moaning as they slowly walk past, we can do something big and global. We can have masses of zombies.' Our approach was to start with the design of that mass, and then, only after we'd come up with that cooler, bigger concept, would we get into 2 / 25 designing individual zombies."

Based on just one of several first-person storylines in Brooks' novel, World War Z opens in Philadelphia, where Gerry Lane (Brad Pitt), a retired United Nations investigator, lives with his wife, Karin (Mireille Enos), and their children. A typical morning turns horrific when zombies attack Philadelphia streets, forcing Gerry to escape the city with his family in a speeding van. Halon had used a special plug-in for driving vehicles when prevising the sequence. "We used an Xbox 360 controller to actually drive the cars so we could get realistic dynamics, like stopping, swerving and crashing," said Daniel Gregoire. "Practically none of that was hand-animated. I tried to reduce the amount of hand animation, so all of it was as realistic as possible." Production shot Philadelphia scenes in Glasgow, Scotland. In post, Cinesite altered and extended Glasgow plates to transform the Scottish city, using stills photographed in 9 / 25 New York and Philadelphia by Matt Johnson and photographer Aviv Yaron. So we were able to use the Glasgow plates for ground interaction - traffic and people walking in front of buildings - but above that were matte-painted and textured CG buildings, based on the photographs. Even if the layout wasn't geographically accurate to Philadelphia, we wanted those recognizable buildings in there." More generic structures topped off some of the Glasgow buildings.We looked for Philadelphia architecture that matched the architecture in Glasgow," related Dyg. ¿Again, those buildings were based purely on the photographs. Very little traditional CG rendering went into it, so it was quite fluid to change things and still keep that photoreal look. We did a lot of this environment work in Nuke. I come from a compositing background, and it just seemed obvious to me that we could use Nuke for a lot of these things that are normally done in Maya or similar 3D packages. I wanted to take them out of that kind of package and into something that was more artist-friendly and could provide a quick turnaround." The escape sequence was roughly a fifty-fifty mix of live-action and animated zombies. 'There is a zombie that attacks Brad on the bicycle," related Scott Farrar, "and that was an animated character. Gerry makes it into the plane and attempts to close the cargo door against an onslaught of zombies.iThe plane that was used to transport the crew and equipment from Malta was actually parked there at Upper Heyford," stated Matt Johnson, "and we have both live and CG characters running toward and into it. "You couldn't shoot something like that for real," commented Scott Farrar. How do you have a slightly lit aircraft taking off in the rain at night with lightning and all of that? That's a case of visual effects telling a part of a story and setting a mood in ways that would be almost impossible to achieve with physical elements." The plane delivers Gerry to Israel, where the government has erected a giant wall around Jerusalem as protection against the zombie invasion. Later in the sequence, thousands of zombies breach the wall by climbing atop one another like ants in a swarm. The Israel sequence had been prevised from beginning to end, prior to the start of production. "We architected that entire sequence," said Daniel Gregoire. "The arc of the se16 / 25 quence was to make us feel safe at first, but then we tease the idea that the wall is

A Tale of Two Cities BY JOE FORDHAM maginative thinkers have long theorized about the possibilities for permanent habitats in space. In the early 20th century, Soviet physicist Konstantin Tsiolkovsky envisioned a city built into a giant rotating space wheel. The concept reappeared - styled after the space art of Chesley Bonestell - in George Pal's 1955 film, Conquest of Space. Fourteen years later, Stanley Kubrick presented a similar orbital construction with unparalleled majesty in 2001: A Space Odyssey. After completing his first feature - the science fiction thriller District 9 - filmmaker Neill Blomkamp hit upon the space wheel concept as a proscenium for his next story. "I was writing a story about wealth discrepancy between the rich and the poori said Blomkamp. "I was trying to figure out how to separate the two, and I found an image that I had been obsessed with since I was a kid. The illustration, created by conceptual artist Syd Mead for National Geographic, depicted the inside of the Stanford Torus - the geometric term for a ring-like, doughnut shape - an early 1970s NASA projection of an agrarian space station, developed at Stanford University. "It had farmlands with robotic 1 / 30 systems harvesting corn crops. All of a sudden, I realized that was it - the rich could

Burnished Steel BY JODY DUNCAN A prominent feature of the marketing campaign for director Richard Donner's 1978 Superman starring the late Christopher Reeve was the rather grandiose claim - 'You'll believe a man can fly.' Well, sort of. Using the Zoptic system - a then state-of-the-art front projection technique - Donner and his effects crews had made significant improvements on the wire rigs and rear projection effects used in the 1960s Superman television series. But premotion control and pre-digital, there were still tremendous limitations to what could be achieved in shots of the ultimate American superhero in flight. The effects artists behind producer Christopher Nolan and director Zack Snyder's Man of Steel - led by visual effects supervisor John 'D.J.' DesJardin - faced no such limitations, and modern technologies enabled them to create the most dynamic Superman yet. A total of 1,500 effects shots divided among four main effects vendors - Weta Digital, MPC, Double Negative and Scanline - served a story penned by Nolan and David Goyer that explored Superman's origins and then transitioned to an existential 1 / 29 battle against a Kryptonian intent on rebuilding his doomed planet's civilization on Earth.

MAN OF STEELI All of the effects facilities were guided by concepts first developed in production designer Alex McDowell's art department and in previsualization by Pixel Liberation Front. "PLF actually started working for the art department before they worked for visual effects," related visual effects producer Josh Jaggars. "They set up a virtual camera system that enabled Zack to move a camera around the sets that Alex was planning to buildi "We built assets very early on so that Zack could immerse himself into environments with his handheld virtual camera," added PLF previs supervisor Kyle Robinson. "We would set up the scene file and the assets, and he could walk around the space and look at everything. We asked him to let us know if there were camera positions or actions he liked, so we could bookmark them and incorporate them into the previs, which we were doing in parallel to working with the art department.i Traditional previs took its cues from Snyder's storyboards, which the director mostly rendered himself, as is his custom. Robinson continued to lead the effort as the PLF team moved into postvis, joining production with the start of principal photography in summer 2011. The shoot continued until early spring 2012, leaving the visual effects vendors a year of postproduction in which to meet the film's June 2013 release date. Rural areas in and around Plano, IIlinois, stood in for Smallville and the Kent farm where Clark Kent grows up, while Chicago represented Metropolis at street level. After shooting those locations, production moved to stages in Vancouver, where crews shot voluminous greenscreen material for fight sequences and scenes set at the North Pole and on Krypton, both of which would be realized primarily as virtual environments. We also went out to Vancouver Island for a couple 2 / 29 of small sequences," related Josh Jaggars. "We shot ocean plates out there for an oil rig

sequence, as well as a crab boat sailing off the coast." A crew from Gentle Giant scanned many blocks of Plano so that it could be recreated digitally for a large battle sequence set in Smallville. iGentle Giant also scanned all of our sets that were built in Vancouver," said Jaggars, "as well as every actor and every stuntman that was going to be re-created digitally." "Entire towns needed to be scanned, not just single sets or props," elaborated Gentle Giant supervisor Steve Chapman. To fill in an entire city, we had to move around to hundreds of different places; and so, each time we did a scan, we would come away with millions of points. With that amount of data, there was no way to just build a big model without coming up with a shortcut. So we took the scan data in 3D and essentially eliminated the Z dimension. From the orbiting Black Zero, Zod launches the World Engine - a massive, powerful machine capable of transforming Earth's landscape into that of Krypton, thus rebuilding the lost planet. The machine lands on Bora Bora, which was an entirely CG environment created by Double Negative, the team awarded most of the visual effects in the film's third act. "The World Engine crashes there," said John DesJardin, "and fires up this energy beam that pulses between Bora Bora and Metropolis on the other side of the world. The beam creates a kind of gravity burst that destroys everything as the World Engine creates Kryptonian terrain. "Knowing that Metropolis had to transform into a surreal Ground Zero wasteland," noted DesJardin, "we thought it would be best to shoot most of the Metropolis sequence on a greenscreen stage, and create the entire environment in CG. We shot some stuff in Chicago, and we took copious photos of the area, so we had that as a base. We also had a lidar scanner on a Spacecam and did scans of city blocks by helicopter. I thought the 24 / 29 helicopter would get us the rooftops and maybe halfway down a building, but it actually

cast all the way down to street level, and we got everything in one connected scan." Double Negative used that scan data to build a massive CG Metropolis - 30 square miles - based on Alex McDowell's designs, which suggested a city that was a hybrid of New York, Los Angeles and Chicago. "Due to the nature of the work," related Double Negative visual effects supervisor Ged Wright,iwe ended up doing the whole thing in 3D. It was one of the biggest CG builds we'd ever had to do; and so, we took a procedural approach to the city. It was complicated, because every environment had to be destructible. As a result, we completely changed how we thought about these shots. We rewrote how we structured all of our assets, and how we rendered them, just because of the sheer amount of data and destruction that we had to do." We shot things like Michael Shannon pretending to grab Henry's cape and spinning him around," added John DesJardin. The goal was to shoot something, but we ended up having to replace most of what was shot, just because of the severity of the action. In that way, it was a big departure for us. Ultimately, given the complexity of the movie and the number of locations, the filmmakers opted to go with the latter. It wasn't just a matter of what it would cost and the effort of shooting native stereo; it was also the fact that the conversions we looked at were so good. No one wanted to deal with cumbersome 3D rigs, and there are always shots you're going to convert anyway. So we decided to make the best traditional 2D movie we could, and then do the 3D conversion later." Tests conducted early in production boosted the filmmakers' confidence in conversion. "We converted a small sequence from 300," recalled Legend stereo visual effects supervisor Jared Sandrew, iand showed that to Zack and producer Debbie Snyder — and they said they were very impressed with the quality of the conversion. After that, we were given some select Man of Steel live-action shots and a couple of visual effects shots that were still works in progress. These were closeups, wide shots, macro lens shots, outer space shots - all different sorts of setups - and we did wedge tests on those, doing three to five different versions of each shot in depth. We showed those to Zack and got a sense of what he wanted this world to look likeii Awarded the assignment, Legend received source plates from the studio, as well as visual effects elements from the effects vendors. "We dug into the vendors' scene files," 27 / 29 recounted Sandrew, '¿and simplified them into various levels of foreground, mid-ground

and background layers. We set up these layers of 2D elements in 3D space. Then we took all of those elements and keyframed them within our proprietary masking process, and sent keyframes to our facility in India to be 'tweened.' While that was happening, our artists in Carlsbad set up the chosen keyframes in stereo, adding internal volume to the elements. The next morning, we got the masks back from India, and put them into the keyframed scene file - so we could immediately see the shots in stereo, that day. Once the sequence is keyframed in our system, we can do anything, which is one of the benefits of stereo conversion. We can easily try a lot of different things, in continuity, to get the exact feel and look we're going for. I think Zack really appreciated that flexibility when developing the stereo look for this film.
